strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful problem: learning low-rank tensors from streaming observations with limited storage. Connecting convergence speed, statistical accuracy, and prediction regret provides a valuable organizing perspective.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the proposed analysis of automatic incoherence preservation and entry-wise accuracy through spectral-projector expansions. This could provide useful new understanding of established Riemannian optimization methods.

Presentation: Explicit algorithms, theorem assumptions, and explanatory discussions make the intended contributions accessible. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges the substantial initialization cost and restrictive binary-learning conditions. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b08/review-experiment-nwtp5drf/call-d371733eb28f49f4bc75e1082ff4f002/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Empirical support: Figure 2 includes ten-trial noise studies supporting the qualitative convergence/error trade-off. Public data sources are identified, and Appendix A transparently reports cases where offline RGrad performs better. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness of the entry-wise guarantee: Appendix G.5, p. 79, drops a stochastic term containing σ sqrt(η) log(d_max)/λ_min when deriving Eq. (69). For fixed ranks, coherence, and condition number with comparable dimensions, the retained noise term is only O(σ sqrt(η)/λ_min). The stated step-size condition cannot absorb this logarithmic difference because both terms scale identically with η. Consequently, the supplied proof does not establish the advertised sharp entry-wise bound in Theorem 6.

Soundness of initialization: Assumption 1 permits nonidentity covariance Σ, but Algorithm 2 and Appendix G.2 use moment identities requiring isotropy. In general, E[Y vec(X)] = Σ vec(T*), so the spectral initialization can target incorrect subspaces even with unlimited observations. Theorem 3 therefore needs stronger design assumptions or a justified covariance correction.

Soundness of concentration arguments: On p. 51, the purported martingale differences multiply centered increments by 1(E_l), although E_l depends on the current covariate X_l. This multiplication generally destroys conditional mean zero, so the stated Azuma-Hoeffding application requires a corrected stopping/truncation argument. Separately, Appendix G.9, p. 98, substitutes the unconditional probability P(Y_t^c) into a conditional Cauchy-Schwarz bound. On histories where the iterate has already left the good set, the conditional failure probability can be one. This leaves the expected-regret guarantees in Theorems 10–11 unsupported by the supplied proof.

Optimality: The lower-bound discussion on pp. 22–23 informally sums offline minimax estimation rates. This does not establish a sequential regret lower bound for a common fixed parameter, particularly when the learner receives an informative warm initialization. Section 6 should also consistently characterize its objective as population prediction pseudo-regret. The headline optimality claim needs a rigorous matching lower bound or an applicable existing result.

Scope and significance: The near-linear completion sample requirement is conditional on initialization, which still requires roughly d^(m/2) observations. Regression initialization also stores an ambient-size tensor. The binary guarantee requires a shrinking signal bound and at least order-d^3 samples. These acknowledged conditions substantially limit the reach of the efficiency claims; acknowledging them is appropriate.

Evaluation: Table 2's prediction errors of 0.018 versus 0.085 are encouraging, but comparison with a model frozen before the changing test period does not isolate the advantage of this particular online method. Persistence, rolling-refit, and competitive online baselines would strengthen the application. The experiments also do not directly test the central entry-wise and incoherence claims or the generalized-linear extensions.

Reproducibility and implementation clarity: Important settings are missing, including simulation initialization sample sizes, the adaptive schedule's initial step size and phase length, and solar-experiment step-size selection. The handling of label availability for the 24-hour forecast should be documented. Algorithm 3 additionally omits the 1/T normalization used in its proof. Pseudocode and public datasets help, but these omissions prevent reliable reproduction.
